title: Performance and memory
summary: Cache repeated work, limit how often handlers run, cancel what keeps running, and count the work a loop does.

concepts.title: Counting the work a loop does

misconceptions.description: Believes a memoized function still runs its body on a repeated input.
Believes that after the first call every later call is served from the cache, whatever the argument.
Believes the cache is created anew on every call, so nothing is remembered.
Believes testing the stored value shows whether an entry exists, even when the value is 0 or another falsy value.
Believes debounce or throttle only delays calls, so every call still runs eventually.
Believes a debounced function runs once after all calls, however long the pauses between them.
Believes a throttle waits until the calls stop and runs only the last one.
Believes any deferring or timer function can stand in for setTimeout inside a debounce.
Believes assigning null to a variable, or adding null somewhere, cancels the timer or callback that already exists.
Believes setInterval runs its callback once at time zero before the first period.
Believes reassigning or clearing a variable frees an object even when another reference still holds it.
Believes a new function with the same body can remove a listener added earlier.
Mixes up which loop or method stops early, or believes every pass always runs.
Believes the work of nested loops adds up, or is counted per loop, instead of multiplying.

conceptCard.title: Remember results by input
conceptCard.body: A function that gives the same answer for the same input can store its answers. Keep a Map outside the call. Look the input up first; do the real work only when it is missing, then store the result. A repeated input costs one lookup.

conceptCard.title: Slow down a busy function
conceptCard.body: Debounce and throttle limit how often a function runs. Debounce waits: each new call cancels the pending timer and starts a new one, so the function runs once after the calls stop. Throttle spaces runs: at most one per interval, the calls in between are dropped.

conceptCard.title: Cancel what you start
conceptCard.body: A timer, a listener or a stored callback keeps working until it is cancelled. Dropping your own variable does not cancel it. Whatever a live callback uses stays reachable. Clear timers by their id, remove listeners by the same function, and empty lists you no longer need.

lessons.title: Counting the work a loop does

conceptCard.title: Count steps, not lines
conceptCard.body: To compare two ways of doing a job, count the steps. Count how many times the loop body runs, not how many lines you wrote. A loop runs once per element, a loop inside a loop runs its inner body once per outer pass, and stopping early saves the rest.

items.prompt: A fruit stall caches its prices by weight. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The body runs for 2 and for 3. The second call for 2 finds the stored price and skips the counter line.
That counts all three calls. A call whose weight is already in the cache returns the stored price without running the counter line.
That treats every call after the first as a hit. The cache is keyed by weight, so the new weight 3 is a miss.

items.explanation: The counter sits inside the if, so it only runs on a cache miss. Weights 2 and 3 are misses; the repeated 2 is a hit and returns the stored price. That makes two runs of the body.
hints: Look at which line increases calls, and when line 4 lets it run.
A memoized function runs its real work only for an input it has not seen.
Compare the three weights: one of them has already been stored by the time it is asked again.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: This program prints 110 twice although tax changed in between. Which statement does it demonstrate?

options.text: A cached answer goes stale when the result also depends on a value outside the arguments.
options.feedback: Right. The cache only knows the argument 100, so it keeps returning the answer stored when tax was 10.

options.text: The second call ran the body again, but it still read the old tax.
options.feedback: If the body had run again it would have read tax as 20 and printed 120. The 110 comes straight from the cache.

options.text: Every call to withTax starts with an empty cache.
options.feedback: The cache is declared outside the function, so it survives between calls. That is why the second call finds the first answer.

items.explanation: Memoization is safe only when the result depends on the arguments alone. Here the result also depends on tax, but the cache is keyed by p only, so after tax changes the stored 110 is returned again.
hints: Compare the two printed numbers with the value of tax at each call.
A cache remembers answers by input; it does not notice other values changing.
Ask where the cache lives and what its key contains.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Order the lines so the visit log prints miss hit: the first check of 7 stores it, the second finds it.
items.explanation: The check reads has before add, so the first call reports a miss and stores the key. Only then can the second call find it. The set may be created before or after the function, but both must come before the calls.
hints: Find the line that reads has and the line that stores the key. Which must come first?
A cache lookup asks the question first and stores the answer afterwards.
The two calls come last, and the printing call is the one that uses the first result.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The warehouse program should print 1 because the second stock(1) hits the cache. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The in operator asks whether the key exists, even when the stored answer is 0.
For a new key seen[k] is undefined, which is not 0, so the function returns undefined before it ever computes anything.
seen.k looks for a property literally named k, which never exists. Nothing is ever read from the cache.

items.explanation: The stored answer for key 1 is 0, and 0 is falsy, so the check treats a stored answer as a miss. Test whether the key exists instead of testing the value.
hints: Check what stock(1) stores, then what line 4 does with that value.
A truthiness test cannot tell a stored 0 from a missing entry.
Ask about the key, not about the stored value.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of cacheMisses(requests). A memoized function is asked for each id in order. Return how many requests it had to compute instead of reading from the cache.
items.explanation: A request is a miss only the first time its id appears. Keep a set of ids already stored; count an id when it is not in the set, then add it.
hints: Think about what must be remembered between requests.
A miss is the first time an id is asked for.
Keep a set of seen ids and count the ids that are not in it yet.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A search box logs a query once typing pauses for 200 ms. Calls arrive at 0, 100 and 400 ms. What does this print?

options.feedback: Right. The call at 100 cancels a, b runs at 300, and c at 400 starts a new wait that nothing interrupts.
That lets every call run. Each new call clears the timer of the previous one if it has not fired yet.
That merges all three calls. b has already fired at 300 because no call arrived during its 200 ms wait.

items.explanation: Each call clears the pending timer and starts a new 200 ms wait. a is cancelled by b at 100. b waits until 300 and runs because nothing arrives before then. c arrives at 400 and runs at 600.
hints: Write down when each call happens and when its timer would fire.
A debounced call is cancelled by any call that arrives before its wait is over.
Check whether the call at 400 comes before or after the timer of the call at 100.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Four calls arrive at the times in the array, and only two lines print. Which statement does this code demonstrate?

options.text: A throttled function runs at most once per interval and ignores the calls in between.
options.feedback: Right. After a run at 0 the calls at 100 and 250 are dropped, and 300 is the first call far enough away.

options.text: It waits until the calls stop and then runs only the last one.
options.feedback: That describes a debounce. This code runs at 0 straight away and never waits for the calls to stop.

options.text: It runs every call, only later.
options.feedback: Calls at 100 and 250 print nothing. They are dropped, not delayed.

items.explanation: A throttle remembers when it last ran. A call runs only if enough time has passed since then, otherwise it is dropped. So 0 and 300 run, and the calls at 100 and 250 do nothing.
hints: Follow lastRun as each time in the array is checked.
A throttle caps how often the function runs; it does not queue the extra calls.
Check which calls print and what the dropped calls had in common.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Fill the blank so the debounced hi forwards its arguments and prints only y after the wait.

options.feedback: Right. A timer waits for the delay, and the next call can cancel it before it fires.
A microtask runs as soon as the current code ends and ignores the delay, so there is nothing for clearTimeout to cancel and both x and y print.
This only cancels; it never schedules fn. Nothing is printed at all.

items.explanation: A debounce needs a cancellable delayed call. setTimeout schedules fn(...args) after wait and returns the id that the next call clears. The arrow keeps args, so the latest arguments reach fn.
hints: Look at what the line must store in t so line 4 can clear it.
Debounce needs a call that waits for a delay and that a later call can cancel.
Pick the function that takes a callback and a delay in milliseconds.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The search should log only find cat, but it logs both queries. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The id of the earlier timer is stored in timer, so that is what must be cleared.
Setting the variable to null only forgets the id. The earlier timer is still scheduled and still fires.
Without an id there is nothing to cancel, so both timers still fire.

items.explanation: clearTimeout needs the id that setTimeout returned. The query string is not an id, so the first timer is never cancelled. Clear the stored id before a new timer is stored.
hints: Compare what line 3 clears with what line 4 stores.
clearTimeout takes the value that setTimeout returned.
The id is kept in a variable declared on line 1.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of throttleRuns(times, gap). A call runs if it is the first, or at least gap after the last run. Return the times that run.
items.explanation: Remember the time of the last call that ran, not the last call. A call runs when it is first or when the gap since that run is at least gap, and only then does the remembered time change.
hints: Decide what must be remembered between calls.
Update the remembered time only when a call actually runs.
The first call always runs, so start from a time infinitely far back.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The page sets poll to null at 250 ms and logs the tick count at 450 ms. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The interval was never cleared, so it still fires at 100, 200, 300 and 400 before the log.
That assumes setting poll to null stopped the interval at 250. The timer system holds the interval, not the variable, so it keeps firing.
That counts a tick at 0. An interval waits one full period before its first run, so the first tick is at 100.

items.explanation: Only clearInterval stops an interval. Assigning null to poll just loses the id, so the interval fires at 100, 200, 300 and 400. The log at 450 sees four ticks.
hints: List the times at which the interval fires.
Changing a variable does not change a timer that was already started.
Count the interval ticks that happen before 450 ms.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The program prints 2. After its last assignment, which statement about the two objects is true?

options.text: Both objects are still reachable, because the history array holds a reference to each.
options.feedback: Right. An object stays alive while any reference reaches it, and the array keeps a reference to each of them.

options.text: Only the object with text b is reachable, because draft moved on from a.
options.feedback: Moving draft away only removes one reference to a. The array was given its own reference on line 2, so a is still reachable.

options.text: Neither object is reachable, because draft is null.
options.feedback: draft was only one of the references. The array still holds both objects, whatever draft contains.

items.explanation: An object can be freed only when nothing reachable refers to it. Reassigning or clearing draft removes one reference at a time. The history array still refers to both objects, so both stay reachable.
hints: Count the places that refer to each object after line 5.
Memory is freed only when no reachable reference is left.
The array was filled before draft changed. What does it still hold?
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Each stored callback keeps its data array reachable. Fill the blank so every stored callback is released and the program prints 0.

options.feedback: Right. Emptying the list drops the callback, and with it the data array it held.
slice returns a copy and leaves jobs unchanged. The callback stays in the list with its data, so the program prints 1.
This adds another entry instead of removing the callback. The list holds two items and the callback still keeps its data.
Calling watch again stores a second callback. The first callback is still in the list with its data.

items.explanation: A callback in a list keeps everything it uses reachable. To release it, remove it from the list. Adding a null entry, calling watch again or copying the list with slice leaves the first callback and its data in place.
hints: Look at what line 3 puts into the list.
Data stays reachable while a stored callback that uses it is still reachable.
Only one chip removes the callback from the list; the others add entries or leave the list as it is.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The tick listener should be removed before the event fires, so hits stays 0. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The set holds the function stored on line 4, and deleting by the same reference removes it.
This is yet another new function. Two functions with the same body are different values, so nothing is removed.
Parentheses call tick, which changes hits and returns a number. The set holds a function, so nothing is removed.

items.explanation: A listener is removed by the same function value that was added. An arrow written again on line 5 is a different function, so the set keeps tick and it still fires. Pass the stored reference.
hints: Compare the value added on line 4 with the value removed on line 5.
Two functions are equal only when they are the very same function.
Remove it by the name it was stored under, without calling it.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of stillRunning(events). Each event is 'start name' or 'stop name' for a timer. Return the names never stopped, in the order they started.
items.explanation: A timer that was stopped no longer runs. Keep the names of running timers: add on start, remove that exact name on stop, and return what is left in start order.
hints: Decide what to keep while reading the events.
A stop must remove the timer it names, not just any timer.
A set keeps insertion order, so spreading it gives start order.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: forEach and find both look at the stops. The counters record how many stops each one visits. What does this print?

options.feedback: Right. forEach visits all six stops. find returns at the third stop, so its callback runs three times.
find stops at the first stop that makes its callback return true. It never visits the stops after the 3.
This swaps the two. forEach always runs for every element, and it is find that quits early.

items.explanation: forEach has no early exit, so its callback runs once per element: six times. find stops at the first match. The 3 is in third position, so visited is 3. Fewer steps means less work.
hints: Count the callback runs separately for each method.
One of the two methods stops as soon as it has its answer.
Find the position of 3 in the list.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: This program prints 16. Which statement about nested loops does it demonstrate?

options.text: The inner body runs once for every pass of the outer loop, so the steps multiply.
options.feedback: Right. Four passes of the outer loop each run the inner body four times: 4 times 4.

options.text: The steps add up: four from the outer loop and four from the inner loop.
options.feedback: That would be 8. The inner loop starts again from the beginning on every outer pass, so its steps are repeated.

options.text: Two loops cost two steps, whatever the lists hold.
options.feedback: Cost is the number of times the body runs, not the number of loops. Each pass over each list adds work.

items.explanation: A loop inside a loop restarts for every pass of the outer loop. With 4 outer passes and 4 inner passes each, the body runs 4 times 4 = 16 times. Count body runs, not loops.
hints: Count how many times line 4 runs for one value of a.
The inner loop starts over on each outer pass.
Multiply the passes of the outer loop by the passes of the inner loop.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Fill the blank so the loop counts ids it has already seen without rescanning a list. The program should print 1.

options.feedback: Right. has answers whether the id is in the set in one step, without scanning the earlier ids.
add returns the set itself, which counts as true for every id. Every id would count as repeated.
Arrays have includes, but a Set does not, so this call fails.

items.explanation: A Set answers membership with has, which does not rescan earlier ids. Only the second 4 is already in the set, so repeated ends at 1.
hints: Look at what the condition on line 5 must ask the set.
Sets have their own method to test membership.
The method name is a short question word about the set.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The search should stop at room b and print 2, but it keeps going. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. break leaves the loop at once, so the later rooms are never visited.
This leaves the loop at the first room that is not b, which is room a, so steps ends at 1.
This sets the counter but the loop still visits c and d, so steps goes on to 4.

items.explanation: continue only skips the rest of the current pass, and nothing follows it. The loop still visits c and d. break ends the loop, so the work stops at room b.
hints: Compare what line 5 does at room b with what you want.
continue skips to the next pass; another keyword leaves the loop.
The loop should end the moment room b is reached.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of pairChecks(list). A duplicate check compares every item with each item after it, with no early exit. Return how many comparisons that makes.

reference: for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
wrongSolutions: for (let j = i; j < n; j++) {

items.explanation: Each item is compared with the items after it only: n - 1, then n - 2, and so on. Count the inner body runs with a nested loop that starts at i + 1.
hints: Count how many items come after the item at position i.
The inner loop should not look backwards or at the item itself.
Start the inner index one step after the outer index.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author
